75 Hard automation

A daily discipline workflow that gathers completion signals, reflections, exercise, water, faith, and date context, then records the structured result in Notion.

Independent workApple Shortcuts · Notion API · Daily accountability

On this page

The frictionThe technical solutionTool responsibilitiesShortcut inventoryRequest structureDependenciesEvidence & limits

The friction

A multi-requirement daily challenge creates repeated cognitive overhead: remembering each requirement, collecting responses, writing reflections, and recording the day consistently. A manual checklist can become another task to maintain.

The technical solution

The Log Discipline Day folder organizes 13 Shortcuts into a daily accountability system. The workflow separates prompts and response helpers from the logging and API layer.

Log Discipline asks for a log date, runs Get Discipline Response, reads Disciplined and Undisciplined values from a dictionary, conditionally combines reflection text, stores a Reflection Response variable, and references water-intake follow-up.

Tool responsibilities

Tool / Responsibility
Tool or data sourceResponsibility
Combat Ready - Last 20 Lbs and Log DisciplineStart the daily accountability flow, collect the log date, and assemble the day’s responses.
Prompt and response ShortcutsSupply morning and milestone messages and collect discipline, reflection, faith, water, and exercise responses.
Discipline Http RequestMap the collected values—including the Date value—into the structured Notion page request.
Notion API and discipline databaseReceive and store the daily record and its Goal Tracker relation; private database and relation identifiers stay unpublished.
Date context and Apple CalendarSupport daily scheduling and accountability. The reviewed request carries its own Date value.
FinchOpen Finch All launches the companion workflow as part of the surrounding accountability setup.

Shortcut inventory

The reviewed folder contains these 13 named Shortcuts:

  1. Combat Ready - Last 20 Lbs — primary shortcut entry point.
  2. Open Finch All — opens the Finch companion workflow.
  3. Get Morning Message — retrieves a morning prompt.
  4. Dynamic Morning Message — prepares a variable morning message.
  5. Get Milestone Message — retrieves milestone context.
  6. Log Discipline — collects and assembles the daily discipline record.
  7. Get Reflections Response — retrieves reflection input.
  8. Get Discipline Response — retrieves disciplined or undisciplined response values.
  9. Get Read Bible Prompt — retrieves the faith/read prompt.
  10. Discipline Http Request — centralizes the Notion API request body.
  11. Get Water Intake — retrieves water-intake completion data.
  12. Get Exercise Response — retrieves exercise completion data.
  13. Log Discipline Day V1 — earlier logging workflow retained in the folder.

Notion request structure

Discipline Http Request receives a dictionary, extracts values for Disciplined, Exercise, Water, Faith, Reflection, and Date, then builds a Notion page request.

The request body includes a date property, a Goal Tracker relation, and structured properties for Disciplined, Exercise Completed, Water Intake, Faith, and Reflection. The database identifier and relation identifiers are intentionally not published.

Application dependencies

  • Apple Shortcuts — runs the prompts, helper workflows, conditional logic, variables, and HTTP request.
  • Notion API — receives the structured daily page request.
  • Notion workspace and database — stores the discipline records and Goal Tracker relation.
  • Notion API integration permissions — required to access the target database.
  • Apple Calendar or date context — useful for daily scheduling and date-based accountability, though the reviewed request body carries its own Date value.
  • Finch — referenced by Open Finch All as part of the surrounding accountability workflow.

Intended benefit

Reduce the mental overhead of repeating a daily checklist, make completion signals consistent, and preserve a searchable record of discipline, exercise, water, faith, reflections, and dates.

The logs also powered a Notion Chart built from the recorded data. Seeing the metrics made effort visible over time and forced a more honest assessment of what I was—or was not—actually completing.

Evidence & current limits

The Shortcut folder and editor review verify the names and behaviors described here. Public screenshots, exported Shortcuts, synthetic request/response examples, and a full run history have not yet been attached.

Next proof-of-work step: show one synthetic daily run from prompt collection through the Notion request while keeping database IDs, relation IDs, API secrets, and personal reflections private. This page documents the workflow; it does not claim a measured adherence improvement.

Apple-native operating system

Redesigning a mixed productivity setup into a coordinated Apple-native system for knowledge, data, tasks, and automation.

Independent workInformation architecture · Migration · Numbers · Shortcuts

On this page

The system behind everyday workGive every tool a defined roleDesign decisions that matteredEvidence & continued refinement

The system behind everyday work

Information was distributed across overlapping productivity tools. Moving to Apple required more than copying notes: the system needed clear ownership for knowledge, structured data, files, tasks, and schedules.

My contribution: workflow analysis, architecture, registries, standards, migration, reusable templates, and automation.

Give every tool a defined role

Apple-native system responsibilities
ToolResponsibility
Apple NotesKnowledge, reference material, and the Guide to GEM Life
NumbersRegistries, structured records, expenses, and dashboards
RemindersTasks, recurring routines, and work queues
CalendarTime-based commitments and scheduling
Shortcuts & SiriStructured capture, retrieval, and repeatable automation
Freeform & iCloudVisual exploration and file storage

Separate content from metadata

The Manual Registry uses stable identifiers, parent-child relationships, record types, navigation references, and statuses. The Tag Registry defines controlled names and classes. This makes the structure explicit instead of leaving it buried in individual notes.

Design decisions that mattered

  • Choose tools by responsibility: use structured tables for data and notes for reference content.
  • Preserve meaning during migration: account for relationships, metadata, and navigation alongside text.
  • Standardize recurring work: use templates, naming conventions, controlled fields, and reusable documentation.
  • Automate after understanding: make the workflow visible before adding another shortcut.

The expense-tracking portion uses XLOOKUP, COUNTIFS, pivot tables, and monthly snapshots. Dictionary-based Shortcuts support structured personal-reference retrieval.

Evidence & continued refinement

This overview is grounded in my documented independent systems work. Redacted registry samples and a guided system walkthrough are not yet published.

Useful next artifacts are a before/after architecture map, a sample parent-child registry, and one task traced from capture through retrieval. Scaffolding Shortcuts will be described in detail after their implementation is reviewed.

An evolving system. The aim is maintainability and practical use; no measured productivity or subscription-savings figure is claimed here.

Dynamic folder structures

An interactive Apple Shortcut that creates a parent folder and a user-defined set of subfolders.

Independent workApple Shortcuts · Variables · Loops · File paths

On this page

A repeatable task worth automatingHow the Shortcut worksGuide & implementation evidenceValidation & lessons

A repeatable task worth automating

Project resources were easier to organize when they started with a clear folder structure. Manually creating a parent folder and multiple issue folders repeated the same setup work each time.

I built an interactive Apple Shortcut and documented the process so the structure could be created from user inputs.

How the Shortcut works

  1. Format the date, if useful. Prepare a date value for the naming convention.
  2. Ask for the main folder name. Store the text input in a variable.
  3. Create the parent folder. Keep its returned folder reference for subsequent actions.
  4. Ask how many subfolders are needed. Use the numeric input as the repeat count.
  5. Repeat the creation step. Ask for each name and create the subfolder inside the stored parent.

The detail that makes it work

The repeated action must use the correct parent folder reference. My guide calls out this dependency when troubleshooting “Unspecified Path” errors.

Guide & implementation evidence

The original guide includes action screenshots, a complete-flow overview, and a comparison of manual and automated setup.

Read the original illustrated guide ↗
Example inputs
Parent: Demo Sprint
Subfolders: 2
Names: Issue A, Issue B

Expected output
Demo Sprint/
  Issue A/
  Issue B/

The example above illustrates the intended output; it is not a captured execution result.

Validation & lessons

The documented validation checks that the parent folder is created, the requested number of subfolders is generated, and each is nested under the correct parent with the supplied name.

Test in a temporary directory before adapting the workflow to real project files. The guide demonstrates variables, repeat control flow, path management, and technical communication without claiming a measured time-saving result.

Hair Care Log

An Apple Shortcuts system that records hair-care activity in Notion, uses Apple Calendar as part of the surrounding workflow, and retrieves prior entries through the Notion API.

Independent workApple Shortcuts · Apple Calendar · Notion API

On this page

The frictionThe technical solutionTool responsibilitiesShortcut actionsApplication dependenciesEvidence & limits

The friction

Hair-care activities, products, styles, conditions, prices, and results are easy to forget or record inconsistently. Finding a previous entry also requires manually searching through a growing Notion log.

The technical solution

Built a modular Apple Shortcuts application connected to a Notion hair-care database. Care Menu is the user-facing entry point. It routes to logging, search, and reusable property helpers rather than placing every decision in one large Shortcut.

The search workflow calls the Notion API, processes returned pages in a loop, builds a title-to-details dictionary containing each log’s readable title, page URL, and date, presents recent entries for selection, and opens the selected Notion page. Apple Calendar is part of the application context for date-based care tracking and review.

Tool responsibilities

Tool / Responsibility
Tool or data sourceResponsibility
Apple Shortcuts — Care Menu, Log Hair Care, Log Hair RetieProvide the entry point and capture hair-care activities for logging.
Search Care Logs and Select Latest Log EntrySearch Notion results, prepare readable titles with page links and dates, and open the selected record.
Hair Care HTTP Request and property helpersMake Notion API requests and read the configured activity, product, image, price, style, condition, and process properties.
Notion API and hair-care databaseSearch and store the structured care-log records; the database remains the source of truth.
Apple CalendarProvides date-based context for care tracking and review; it is not represented as the log database.
Notion integration and property schemaGrant access to the required pages and database and keep helper names and data types aligned, without publishing credentials or private IDs.

Shortcut actions

The Hair Care Log folder contains these 18 named Shortcuts:

  1. Care Menu — central user-facing router.
  2. Log Hair Care — records a hair-care activity.
  3. Log Hair Retie — records a retie event.
  4. Search Care Logs — searches existing Notion records.
  5. Select Latest Log Entry — presents recent entries for selection.
  6. Hair Care HTTP Request — centralizes Notion API request behavior.
  7. Get Care Activity — retrieves the activity property.
  8. Get Products — retrieves products associated with a log.
  9. Get Product Images — retrieves product image data.
  10. Get Product Price — retrieves product price data.
  11. Get Product Type — retrieves product type data.
  12. Add Pros To Product — adds product advantages to a record.
  13. Add Cons To Product — adds product drawbacks to a record.
  14. Get Hair Style — retrieves the hair-style property.
  15. Get Hair Style 2 — supports a second style value or style branch.
  16. Get Initial Condition — retrieves the starting condition.
  17. Get Completed Condition — retrieves the ending condition.
  18. Get Process Type — retrieves the process classification.

Application dependencies

  • Apple Shortcuts — runs the menu, logging, search, parsing, selection, and property-retrieval workflows.
  • Apple Calendar — provides date-based context for care activity tracking and review.
  • Notion API — searches the care-log database, reads page properties, and opens the selected page.
  • Notion workspace and hair-care database — stores the searchable source-of-truth records.
  • Notion API integration — must have access to the relevant database and pages.
  • Consistent Notion property names and types — required by the property helper Shortcuts.
  • Secure API-key handling and permissions — required for authenticated requests without exposing credentials.

Intended benefit

Reduce the cognitive load of maintaining a long-term hair-care record, make previous entries easier to retrieve, and create more consistent data for reviewing products, routines, styles, and outcomes.

Evidence & current limits

The reviewed workflow documentation establishes the 18-Shortcut structure and the Notion search behavior described here. Public screenshots, exported Shortcuts, synthetic API request and response examples, and the database schema with private identifiers removed have not yet been attached.

Next proof-of-work step: show one new care entry, one Notion search, and retrieval of a previous log while keeping API keys, page IDs, and personal records private.

API integration · Documented in 2024

Notion API integration

Reducing repetitive setup for service-account pages and databases in Notion—while keeping the custom icons, banners, and structure I wanted.

Independent workREST APIs · JSON · Dictionaries · Technical documentation

On this page

Keep the customization. Reduce the repetition.Toolkit architectureSetup & permissionsParsing & portabilityInspect the documented workflowHistorical implementation, lasting lessons

Keep the customization. Reduce the repetition.

I wanted dedicated Notion pages for my service accounts, each with its own supporting database and customized presentation. But creating each one meant repeating the same setup: page and database structures, annual log pages, icons, and banners. I was spending hours customizing them.

The goal was to reduce that redundancy without giving up the customization. I built reusable Apple Shortcuts to collect the details that changed between service accounts and create the repeated structure through the Notion API.

A modular toolkit, not a single request

I separated recurring work into 14 Shortcuts: URL intake and ID extraction, authentication preparation, database and page operations, and reusable property formatters. The design favors reusable components and standardized inputs instead of one-off workflows for each task.

From a shared link to an API target

The parsing feeds the identifiers used by the Notion API; the workflow separates link normalization from the schema-specific request payload.

Get DB or Page ID accepts Apps and URLs through the Share Sheet, then branches between page and database share links. The page path splits on hyphens and takes the final segment; the database path splits on gemsforge/ and takes the second item. A replacement step removes query-string content.

This makes shared links usable as API targets without manually copying identifiers. The parsing is tailored to the URL formats used in this implementation.

Reuse authentication preparation

Create Database and Create DB Pages both call Get Notion Api Key before sending requests. A common helper prepares authentication details for higher-level workflows.

Build structured property payloads

Dedicated formatters prepare JSON-compatible fragments for text, select, multi-select, and relation properties. The color-aware multi-select formatter initializes an array, loops through selected values, conditionally calls Get Color, and assembles objects for the API payload.

Compose the higher-level operations

  • Create Database: requests to https://api.notion.com/v1/databases.
  • Create DB Pages: requests to https://api.notion.com/v1/pages.
  • Search Page properties and Update Page Property: additional toolkit workflows for inspecting and changing properties.
  • Get Icon And Banner: customized presentation resources.
View all 14 workflows

  • Get ID
  • Get Notion Api Key
  • Create Database
  • Create DB Pages
  • Search Page properties
  • Update Page Property
  • Format Text property
  • Format Select Property
  • Format Multi Select Property
  • Format Multi Select Property W/Color
  • Format Relation property
  • Get Color
  • Get Icon And Banner

Integration setup & permissions

The workflow requires a task-specific Notion integration, its integration secret, and explicit access to the target page or database. The target must be shared with the relevant integration; a URL or identifier alone does not grant access.

The secret must be supplied securely and excluded from shared workflow artifacts, screenshots, and source examples. This portfolio describes the authentication dependency without exposing credential values.

Parsing decisions & portability

The database-ID parser depends on a gemsforge/ URL segment, while the page parser uses a more general final-segment approach. Supporting other workspaces or link formats would require reviewing that assumption.

The Shortcut explicitly notes unreliable regex behavior in its fallback path. The implementation combines branching, string splitting, and replacement rather than assuming one expression handles every link.

These are documented limitations, not claims of universal URL support. A fresh compatibility check should cover current link formats, query parameters, and the applicable Notion API version.

Inspect the documented workflow

A small example of structured property mapping

These Shortcuts act as a lightweight serialization layer: they transform friendly Shortcut inputs into typed Notion API property objects before a create-page or update-page request is sent.

Color-aware multi-select

// Friendly input
{
  "name": "Research",
  "color": "blue"
}

// Notion-compatible payload
{
  "Tags": {
    "multi_select": [
      { "name": "Research", "color": "blue" }
    ]
  }
}

Format Multi Select Property W/Color initializes an array, loops through selected values, extracts each name, checks for a color, calls Get Color when needed, and builds the final JSON-ready objects.

Other typed mappings

These dictionaries follow Notion’s property object schema, which I used as the reference while designing the Shortcut mappings.

// Select
{
  "Status": { "select": { "name": "In progress" } }
}

// Relation
{
  "Related project": {
    "relation": [{ "id": "notion-page-or-database-id" }]
  }
}

// Rich text
{
  "Description": {
    "rich_text": [{
      "type": "text",
      "text": { "content": "Project notes" }
    }]
  }
}
{
  "Status": { "select": { "name": "Due ⚠️" } },
  "Year": { "select": { "name": "2025" } }
}

Excerpt adapted from the documented 2024 request body. It illustrates the mapping approach, not a complete request or a current API compatibility guarantee.

Historical implementation, lasting lessons

Documented in 2024. API structures and capabilities change. This is a project account, not a verified current setup tutorial. Shared Shortcuts and present-day compatibility have not been retested.

The enduring work is the modular dependency chain: shared-link intake, target ID extraction, reusable authentication preparation, typed property fragments, and higher-level API operations. The next step is a fresh demonstration with sample data and current API documentation.
